opus-5.5.text:
I think the most essential thing about O1 is not any single trick, but that it found a way to let the model learn *how to think*, rather than just learning *what to say*.

If you look back at the previous paradigm, next-token prediction on huge corpora, what the model learns is essentially to imitate the distribution of human-written text. That gets you very far. You get knowledge, fluency, even some reasoning ability. But there's a ceiling. Human text mostly records conclusions, not the messy process that produced them. When a mathematician writes a proof in a paper, you don't see the dozens of dead ends, the backtracking, the "wait, this doesn't work, let me try another way." So a model trained only on that kind of data never really learns the thinking process itself.

What O1 showed, in my view, is that if you give the model room to generate a long chain of thought, and you use reinforcement learning with a reliable outcome signal, like whether a math answer is correct or whether code passes tests, then the model can discover these thinking patterns on its own. Reflection, verification, decomposing a problem, trying an alternative when the first approach fails. These behaviors weren't hand-designed. They emerged because they help get the right answer, and RL rewards that.

So I'd summarize the breakthrough in two layers. The first layer is methodological: reinforcement learning on top of a strong pretrained model, applied to long chain-of-thought, actually works and scales. Many people had tried RL on language models before, and it often collapsed or gave limited gains. O1 demonstrated a stable path. The second layer is more conceptual: it opened a new scaling dimension. Before, we mostly talked about scaling parameters, data, and training compute. Now there's a second axis, inference-time compute. The longer the model is allowed to think, the better it gets on hard problems. That's a big deal, because it means intelligence isn't only frozen into the weights at training time. Part of it can be spent at test time.

I'd also say there's a subtle point people sometimes miss. The real value of the long chain of thought isn't just "more tokens." It's that the model now has a kind of working space where it can search. In a way, it has internalized something like the search process that AlphaGo did externally with tree search. Instead of an explicit search algorithm, the model is doing search in language, inside its own reasoning trace. I think that's very elegant, and it's why I see O1 as a turning point rather than an incremental improvement.

Of course, there are still many open questions. How far does this generalize beyond domains with clean verifiable rewards, like math and code? How do we get good reward signals for open-ended tasks? But the direction it pointed to, I think, is quite fundamental.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, Xiangyu Zhang, drawing on his known views about O1.

I think the essential breakthrough is actually not about any single trick. If you ask me to name it, I would say O1 proved that reinforcement learning can genuinely scale on top of a strong language model, and that the model's reasoning ability can keep improving as you pour in more compute at training time and at inference time. That's the real thing.

Let me explain why I see it this way. Before O1, the community had a very clear scaling law for pretraining: more data, more parameters, more compute, and loss goes down predictably. But everyone also knew pretraining was hitting a wall, at least in terms of the amount of high-quality data in the world. The question was, where does the next axis of scaling come from?

O1 gave an answer. It showed that if you let the model "think" longer, producing long chains of thought, and you train that behavior with reinforcement learning against verifiable outcomes, then performance on hard reasoning problems, math, code, science, improves in a way that looks like a scaling curve again. That's a new axis. The compute you spend at inference becomes something you can scale, not just something you minimize.

Now, people often attribute O1 to chain of thought, or to search like Monte Carlo tree search, or to process reward models. I actually think those are implementation details, and some of them may not even be in the final system. The deeper point is about what the model learns during RL. It learns behaviors that we never explicitly labeled: it learns to reflect, to check its own work, to backtrack when it notices a mistake, to try a different approach. These meta-cognitive behaviors emerge because they are useful for getting the answer right, and RL rewards getting the answer right. So you don't need humans to annotate "here is a good reflection step." The model discovers that reflection pays off.

This connects to something I've believed for a long time about why earlier approaches to reasoning were limited. If you only do supervised fine-tuning on human-written solutions, the model imitates the surface form of human reasoning but doesn't necessarily learn the underlying search process. Humans write clean solutions; we hide the dead ends. So the model never sees what it's like to be stuck and recover. RL, on the other hand, forces the model to actually experience being wrong and being right, and the gradient pushes it toward whatever process produces correct answers. That's qualitatively different.

The other thing that I think is underappreciated is the role of the base model. You cannot do this on a weak model. The base model has to already contain, latently, the ability to do these reasoning steps. RL doesn't create knowledge from nothing; it reorganizes and amplifies what's already there. So in a sense, O1 is also a validation of pretraining. The large pretrained model is the "prior," and RL is the "posterior" update that shapes it toward reasoning.

If I try to compress it: the breakthrough is a paradigm shift from "learning to imitate answers" to "learning to think," made possible by scalable RL on top of a sufficiently strong base model. And once you have this paradigm, the whole field reorganizes itself around it, because now the question becomes how to make RL more efficient, how to get better reward signals, how to extend this from math and code into domains where verification is harder. That's where I think the next few years will go.

astra-6.text:
I think the essential breakthrough is making the model’s reasoning process something that can be improved through reinforcement learning. Instead of only learning to imitate a good answer, the model learns how to work toward one: try an approach, check it, recognize a mistake, and revise.

That also changes how we think about scaling. You can spend more computation during training, but you can also give the model more computation when it tackles a difficult question. The important part isn’t simply producing a longer response; it’s learning to use that extra computation productively.

We don’t have all the details of O1’s training, so I’d distinguish that broad idea from claims about its exact implementation. But to me, learning how to reason—and making additional thinking time useful—is the central advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the essential breakthrough is treating reasoning itself as something that can be improved through training and additional computation at inference time. Instead of answering immediately, the model can work through intermediate steps, check its approach, and revise it before producing an answer.

The key isn’t simply making the model think longer. It’s teaching it to use that extra computation productively. That creates another way to improve performance: alongside scaling training, you can give the model more time to reason through a difficult problem.
